title: Code & Coffee
description: Dave Carrow writes about servers, county networking, and things he has measured in Verity County.

data.author: Dave Carrow
data.tagline: a Gridfall sysadmin types things after work
data.about:
I do desktop and server support for the Verity County school district and I run a small amount of hardware in my basement in Tannery Flats. I am not a programmer by training. I did two years at the community college in Ardo and then the fastener plant needed somebody to keep the inventory machine running and that was 1997 and here we are.

Everything here is what I actually did on my own equipment. If I am guessing I will say I am guessing. If I am wrong, tell me in the comments and I will correct the post and leave a note saying I corrected it.

posts.title: The homelab, such as it is
posts.body:
People on the boards keep asking what I run, mostly so they can tell me it is wrong. Here it is.

[b]The hardware[/b]

[list][*]A tower that was a district desktop until 2005. 2.4 GHz, 1 GB, two 160 GB drives in software RAID 1. This is the file server and it does everything important.[*]A second tower, older, 512 MB, one disk. This is the thing I break on purpose.[*]A 100 Mbit switch on a shelf.[*]An external drive that lives at my sister's house in Pell and comes home every fourth Sunday. That is the offsite backup and it is the only part of this I would defend in front of a professional.[/list]

No rack. The whole thing is on a workbench with a piece of plywood over the top so nothing drips on it, because the basement in Tannery Flats does what basements in Tannery Flats do.

[b]The software[/b]

Debian on both. Samba for the shares because the house has two Windows machines. Postfix for local mail only, not accepting anything from outside, because I do not want to be in the mail business. Apache serving one virtual host, this one, and a local mirror of a few things I read.

[b]The part that took the longest[/b]

Power. Two outlets on one fifteen amp circuit that also has the chest freezer on it. The freezer compressor kicking in was dropping the older tower about once a week until I moved it to the circuit that comes off the other side of the panel.

That sounds like a joke about the county grid and it is not, it is my house wiring, which is from 1961 and which I am not touching.

The UPS is a consumer unit that gives me about nine minutes. Nine minutes is enough to shut down cleanly if I am home. If I am not home, the file server has been power cycled uncleanly maybe fifteen times since 2005 and the RAID has never had anything to say about it, which I attribute to luck and not to my planning.

[b]What I would do differently[/b]

Buy the second disk at the same time as the first. I ran that server on one drive for eleven months telling myself I would get to it.

comments.author: kupfer_r
comments.body: Software RAID 1 on a machine with no ECC is a false sense of security. You are protected against a disk dying and against nothing else.

comments.author: d.carrow
comments.body: That is fair and I agree with all of it. It is protection against the failure mode I have actually had twice, which is a disk dying. The offsite drive covers the rest badly.

comments.author: marla
comments.body: I understood the part about the freezer.

posts.title: Against Cinderblock CMS
posts.body:
The district bought Cinderblock in 2005 on a three year contract. I have been the person who administers it since the day it was installed. I would like to write down why it is bad while the contract is still in force, because in 2008 nobody will believe me that it was this bad.

[b]One. It stores markup in the database and it stores it badly.[/b]

Every page body is a single text column containing HTML that the editor generated. The editor generates different HTML depending on which browser the secretary was using. I have four variants of the same bulleted list in the same table because four different people made four different lists.

[b]Two. There is no export.[/b]

There is a backup. The backup is a proprietary archive that only Cinderblock can read. When I asked the vendor for a documented export format the answer was that export is available in the Enterprise tier.

The entire point of a content management system is that the content outlives the system. A CMS with no export is a hostage situation with a login screen.

[b]Three. It sends mail as the logged-in user from the server, with no way to change the envelope sender.[/b]

I spent two days in 2006 explaining to a high school principal why messages she sent were arriving in junk folders. The answer was that the software is wrong. There was nothing to do about it.

[b]Four. Page load.[/b]

The district home page issues fourteen database queries to render a menu that has not changed since 2005. I know it is fourteen because I turned on the query log for a day and then turned it off again because the query log filled the disk.

[b]What I actually want[/b]

Files. Text files in a directory, one per page, in some markup a person can read with their eyes. A script that turns them into HTML. Version control, which for a school district could reasonably be a directory called old.

That is not a product anybody sells to a school district, because you cannot put a per-seat license on a directory.

The contract is up in August 2008. I have started the memo now because it will take me that long to get it read.

comments.author: a.rusk
comments.body: Dave, if you write that memo in the form of a cost comparison rather than a list of grievances I will put it in front of the board. I mean that seriously.

comments.author: d.carrow
comments.body: Noted and I will. The grievance version was for here.

comments.author: webmaster_hs
comments.body: Fourteen queries for a static menu is not a CMS problem, it is a caching problem, and you could fix it in an afternoon with a generated include. Blaming the vendor for something you have not tried to fix is lazy.

comments.author: d.carrow
comments.body: I cannot put a generated include in front of it because the template is stored in the database and the vendor support agreement voids if the template table is modified. That is in the contract. I have read the contract more times than the vendor has.

posts.title: Why I left the VRHS mailing list
posts.body:
I unsubscribed from the Verity Regional Historical Society technology list on Thursday after four years. A couple of people asked why, so here it is once and then I am done with the subject.

The list was set up in 2003 to coordinate scanning the society's photograph collection. That was a good project. We scanned about 2,400 items. I wrote the naming convention and the little script that built the index page, and I do not regret one hour of it.

Somewhere around 2005 the list stopped being about scanning.

What it became was a place where three people relitigate the substation fire. Every thread. A question about TIFF compression becomes a thread about the 2003 outage by the fourth reply. I am not exaggerating for effect, I went back through my archive before writing this and it happens in roughly one thread in three.

I do not think those three people are bad. Two of them lost freezers full of food and one of them has a genuine unresolved complaint with the utility about his service drop. Those are real. They are also not about TIFF compression.

I raised it twice, politely, off-list, to the list owner. The response both times was that the list is unmoderated by design and that anybody is free to skip messages.

That is a legitimate position for a list owner to take. It is also a position that means the list will be whatever the three most persistent people want it to be.

So: unsubscribed. The scanning index will keep working. It is static HTML and it has no dependencies and the society can move it to any machine that serves files.

If people want to argue about the transformers there is an entire board for that at [url=synth://boards.gridfall.net/]boards.gridfall.net[/url] where the argument has been running since June 2003 and where I am told it is now in its ninth hundred reply.

I will still scan things. Call the house.

comments.author: H. Speltz
comments.body: As collections chair I am sorry it went this way and I do not blame you. The list was my idea and I have not moderated it because I did not want to be the person who deletes a neighbor's message. That has turned out to be its own decision.

comments.author: Carl B.
comments.body: I am obviously one of the three. I will say that my service drop is a real problem and that I have never once brought it up in a thread that was not already off topic. The other two I will not speak for.

comments.author: d.carrow
comments.body: Carl, your drop is a real problem and you have been more reasonable about it than anybody would be in your position. I checked the archive before I posted and you are right, you are not the worst offender. I should have said that in the post and I am saying it now.

posts.title: Mirroring a site for offline reading
posts.body:
Half the county is on dial-up and the other half has a connection that goes away when it rains. I keep local copies of a handful of sites I read so that I can read them at four in the morning during an outage, which is when I am usually awake and never online.

This is what I do. It is not clever. It works.

[b]1. Decide what you actually want[/b]

Not the whole site. A site with a calendar or a search form will generate infinite URLs and you will wake up to a full disk. Mirror the parts you read.

[b]2. Pull it[/b]

[code]
#!/bin/sh
# mirror-one.sh  -- pull one site into /srv/mirror/<name>
NAME="$1"
BASE="$2"
DEST="/srv/mirror/$NAME"

mkdir -p "$DEST"
wget \
  --mirror \
  --page-requisites \
  --convert-links \
  --adjust-extension \
  --no-parent \
  --wait=2 \
  --random-wait \
  --reject-regex '(\?s=|/search|/calendar)' \
  --directory-prefix="$DEST" \
  "$BASE"
[/code]

The two flags that matter for not being a nuisance are the wait and the random wait. These are small sites run by one person on a cheap host. Two seconds between requests costs you nothing and costs them nothing.

The reject-regex is where you put the traps you have found. Mine has grown every time I have filled a disk.

[b]3. Keep the old copy until the new one finishes[/b]

[code]
# rotate, so a failed run does not leave you with nothing
rsync -a --delete /srv/mirror/$NAME/ /srv/mirror/.$NAME.new/
# ... run wget into .$NAME.new ...
if [ -s "/srv/mirror/.$NAME.new/index.html" ]; then
    rm -rf "/srv/mirror/.$NAME.old"
    mv "/srv/mirror/$NAME"      "/srv/mirror/.$NAME.old"
    mv "/srv/mirror/.$NAME.new" "/srv/mirror/$NAME"
fi
[/code]

The test on index.html is crude. It has still saved me twice, both times when the far end was down and wget cheerfully produced a directory of nothing.

[b]4. Run it at a sane hour[/b]

[code]
# crontab -e
17 3 * * 2  /usr/local/bin/mirror-one.sh kestrel  <base url of the site>
41 3 * * 4  /usr/local/bin/mirror-one.sh county    <base url of the site>
[/code]

Use a minute that is not zero. Everybody uses zero.

[b]5. Serve it locally[/b]

One Apache alias per mirror, nothing fancy:

[code]
Alias /m/ /srv/mirror/
<Directory /srv/mirror>
    Options Indexes FollowSymLinks
    AllowOverride None
    Order allow,deny
    Allow from 192.168.1.0/24
</Directory>
[/code]

That last line is the important one. Do not serve your mirror of somebody else's site to the world. You are keeping a copy for yourself, which is a normal thing to do, and you are not becoming a second copy of their site, which is not.

[b]The reason I bother[/b]

The [url=synth://kestrel-journal.net/]kestrel journal[/url] stopped updating in 2005. One day its host will stop paying. I have every post on a disk in my basement and a copy of that disk at my sister's house in Pell, and when the original goes away I will write to the author and ask what she wants done with it.

That is the whole argument for local copies. Not bandwidth. Not dial-up. The web deletes things.

comments.author: kupfer_r
comments.body: The index.html size test will pass on a soft 404 page. Check for a string you expect on the real page instead.

comments.author: d.carrow
comments.body: Correct and I have changed mine to grep for a string. Leaving the post as written with this note, because the version above is what I actually ran for two years and somebody should see the flaw.

comments.author: marla
comments.body: the last paragraph. yes. I have been saying this about photographs since 2004 and nobody listens until it is gone.

posts.title: I put a receiver on the Signal on 62
posts.body:
Preamble, because I know how this is going to be read.

I do not think there is a numbers station on Route 62. I think there is something on Route 62 that people have been hearing since about 1998 and that nobody local has measured, and measuring things is a hobby I have. That is the entire motivation. If you are hoping for a spooky post you are going to be disappointed and I would rather disappoint you in paragraph two than in paragraph twenty.

[b]What people report[/b]

The usual account: driving the stretch of Route 62 between the Bracken Lane intersection and the quarry entrance, roughly four miles, late at night, AM radio, and between stations you get a voice reading groups of digits. Most accounts say five digit groups. Most say a woman's voice. A lot of accounts say it is clearer in winter and several say it is clearer during power outages, which is the detail that made me interested rather than bored.

[b]What I used[/b]

A surplus receiver and a laptop with a sound card, a long wire on a fiberglass mast clamped to the truck, and a notebook. This is not proper test equipment. I am aware. A spectrum analyzer is not a thing a school district desktop tech owns.

[b]What I did[/b]

Eleven trips between September 8 and October 27. Six of them between midnight and 3 a.m. I drove the four mile stretch at 35 mph with the receiver scanning, stopping at half mile marks, logging the time, the temperature, and anything I heard.

[b]What I got[/b]

On four of eleven trips I recorded a voice reading digits. It is real. It is on tape. I will put a clip up once I have a host that will take the file.

Here is the part nobody wants.

It was on 1610 kHz all four times. That is the top of the AM broadcast band, where the travelers' information stations live. The county runs a TIS transmitter at the fairgrounds on Route 62, licensed, ten watts, and it has run a loop about fair parking and road closures since the 1990s.

That does not explain digits. But on the night of October 27 I recorded the digits and then, forty seconds later, the same voice said what I am fairly confident is "lot C" before going back to digits.

My current best guess, stated as a guess: the TIS loop equipment is old, it is playing a recorded announcement that includes a sequence of numbers, possibly a phone number or a set of frequencies or a date read digit by digit, and the loop is damaged or the tape is worn so you get fragments out of order. Fragments out of order sound exactly like a numbers station. That is not a coincidence, it is what a numbers station is.

[b]The things that do not fit[/b]

I am not going to hide these.

[list][*]Three of the four receptions were at a point about 2.8 miles from the fairgrounds transmitter, and reception at the fairgrounds itself was clean loop audio with no digits. Ten watts on 1610 should be strongest at the source.[*]Two of the four were during a period when the county says the TIS was off for the season. I have that in writing from the roads department and I believe them.[*]The winter and outage correlation in the folklore, if it is real, points at propagation or at something on the distribution line, not at a licensed transmitter.[/list]

So I have a plausible mechanism that explains the content and does not explain the geography or the timing.

[b]What would settle it[/b]

Two receivers, a known separation, and a bearing. I do not have two receivers. If somebody in the county has a second setup and wants to sit at the Bracken Lane end while I sit at the quarry end on the same night, write to me.

[b]What I am not claiming[/b]

That it is the substation. That it is the government. That it stopped in 2004, which I have seen asserted and which is false because I recorded it three weeks ago.

The county wiki has a page on this at [url=synth://wiki.gridfall.net/]wiki.gridfall.net[/url] and it is, to be polite, contested. People have also posted recordings to [url=synth://clipvault.tv/]clipvault.tv[/url], most of which are somebody's cousin doing a voice.

comments.author: 62listener
comments.body: You drove it eleven times in the fall with a wire on a truck and you think you have explained something people have heard for ten years. The TIS answer has been floated and knocked down on the boards twice. You did not read the thread. You did not ask anybody. You just wanted a post.

comments.author: d.carrow
comments.body: I read the thread. I have the print of it in a binder. The TIS theory was floated in 2004 by somebody who never took a receiver out there, and knocked down by people who also never took a receiver out there. I am not saying I explained it. I wrote three paragraphs saying what does not fit. If you have logs, post them and I will take them seriously.

comments.author: 62listener
comments.body: I do not keep logs. I have heard it nine times since 1999 and I know what I heard.

comments.author: kupfer_r
comments.body: The 2.8 mile null is interesting on its own. Ground conductivity out by the quarry is going to be poor and you could easily get a reflection off the tailings face. Worth measuring even if the rest goes nowhere.

comments.author: Carl B.
comments.body: Try it during an outage. Everybody who has heard it clearly has heard it when the lights were out. I know how that sounds. It is still what people say.

posts.title: Follow-up: no, it is not the substation
posts.body:
The last post got more traffic than everything else on this site put together and about a third of the replies said some version of "it is the substation." So, briefly.

[b]The claim[/b]

That Gridfall Substation No. 3, or the distribution line running out Route 62 from it, is producing the signal, and that this is why people hear it during outages and in cold weather.

[b]Why it does not work[/b]

Power equipment does make radio noise. Corona on a high voltage line, a cracked insulator, an arcing connector: all of these produce broadband noise across the AM band and they are worse in humidity and worse when hardware is degraded. That part of the folklore is sound, and it is probably why people who live near lines think their radios are haunted.

Broadband noise is a buzz or a rasp. It is not speech.

To get speech out of a power line you need something that is already speech, modulated onto something. A faulty connector can rectify a nearby broadcast signal and re-radiate it, which is a real and documented effect, and that gets you speech. But the speech you get is whatever station is strong at that spot. It is not novel content. Nobody is generating new audio in a transformer.

So the substation can plausibly explain the noise and can plausibly explain re-radiating something. It cannot explain digits that do not appear on any station.

[b]The outage correlation[/b]

I took Carl's suggestion seriously and I had an opportunity on November 14 when the Hollis Road circuit was out for about three hours for scheduled work. I drove the stretch twice. Nothing. Clean band, quieter than usual, which is what you would expect with the line dead.

One trip is one trip. But if the signal required the outage, that was the night for it.

My suspicion about the outage folklore is ordinary: during an outage you are driving a dark road with nothing else to do and the radio on, and the band is quieter so weak things are audible, and you are paying attention. All three of those make you more likely to hear something that was there all along.

[b]Still open[/b]

The 2.8 mile business. kupfer_r's reflection idea is the best suggestion anybody made and I do not have the equipment to test it.

[b]Correction[/b]

In the last post I wrote that the county TIS is ten watts. The license is for ten watts effective radiated power, which is not the same as ten watts out of the box, and I should not have written it the way I did. Thank you to the person who wrote to me about it, who was polite about it, which I noticed.

[b]Housekeeping[/b]

I am not posting the recordings on [url=synth://clipvault.tv/]clipvault.tv[/url] after all. Two people have already posted edits of other people's recordings there with added reverb. I will send the raw files to anybody who asks and who tells me what they intend to do with them.

comments.author: Carl B.
comments.body: You went out and tried it. That is more than anybody else has done in ten years. I still think you will get it during an unplanned outage in February and not during scheduled work in November.

comments.author: 62listener
comments.body: One trip. One. And a paragraph explaining to the county why we are all imagining things.

comments.author: kupfer_r
comments.body: If you can borrow a portable with an internal ferrite you can get a rough bearing by nulling it. Not a real direction find but it would tell you whether the thing is toward the quarry face or toward the fairgrounds, and that is the whole question.

posts.title: Six months of voltage logs from the Gridfall feeder
posts.body:
Since June I have had a logger on an outlet in the basement recording RMS voltage once a minute. 261,000 samples and change. This is what is in them.

[b]Setup[/b]

A consumer power monitor that talks serial, a script that writes one line per minute to a CSV, and a nightly job that rolls the file. The monitor is not calibrated against anything. Absolute numbers from it mean little. Changes over time mean something.

[b]The headline[/b]

Nominal sits between 119 and 122 almost all the time. Boring, which is the correct answer for a power system.

There were 47 sags below 110 V lasting more than one sample. Forty-one of those are between 5:40 and 6:10 in the evening, which is the freezer and the well pump in the same house, and I can match them to the appliance because they stop when the freezer is unplugged. That is my problem and not the utility's.

That leaves six.

[b]The six[/b]

Four line up with weather. Two of those are the June thunderstorm and one is the September wind.

Two do not line up with anything I can find: August 3 at 2:14 a.m. and November 9 at 3:31 a.m. Both about four minutes, both down to around 104.

I checked whether the roads department or the utility had anything scheduled. Nothing published.

[b]What this is worth[/b]

Almost nothing, and I want to be clear about that because the boards will take it somewhere I did not.

One uncalibrated meter, one outlet, one house, in Tannery Flats, which is not the Depot Street circuit that everybody argues about. If you want to know whether people near the substation have worse service than people elsewhere, the experiment is five loggers on five circuits for a year, and it needs somebody to buy five loggers.

I have offered to lend mine to anybody on Depot Street who will plug it in and leave it alone for three months. The offer stands. It has been taken up once and then the person moved.

[b]The data[/b]

The CSVs are on the file server. If you want them, ask and I will put a copy on a disc. They are about 14 MB uncompressed and about 900 KB zipped, because it is six months of nearly identical numbers.

comments.author: Carl B.
comments.body: I will take the logger. I am on Depot Street, I am retired, and I will not touch it. Call the house.

comments.author: d.carrow
comments.body: Carl it is yours. I will bring it Saturday. One condition: three months, and whatever it says, we publish it. Including if it says your service is fine.

comments.author: Carl B.
comments.body: Agreed and that is the only fair way to do it.

posts.title: Photographing the branch before they lift it
posts.body:
The Gridfall branch closed in March 2007. The rails are still down. The abandonment is approved, the rail-banking application is somewhere in a state office, and at some point a contractor is going to arrive with a machine and it will take about three weeks.

I have been photographing it on weekends since October. Not artistically. Systematically, which is a different job and which nobody else appears to be doing.

[b]The method[/b]

Every public grade crossing and every bridge, photographed from four positions: both approaches along the track, and both approaches along the road. Same four every time. A whiteboard in the first frame of each set with the date and the location so I do not have to trust the file dates.

That is nineteen locations and seventy-six photographs per pass. I have done four passes. The fourth was in snow and is the best one.

[b]Why four positions and not one nice picture[/b]

Because in 1997 somebody photographed the tannery before it came down and took thirty beautiful photographs of the front elevation and none at all of the loading dock, and when the historical society wanted to know how the siding entered the building nobody could answer it. I have watched that happen. A record is not a portfolio.

[b]The boring details that matter[/b]

Shoot everything at the highest setting the camera has, even though the files are large and the card fills. Storage gets cheaper. The train does not come back.

Write the location on paper in the frame. EXIF gets stripped by every piece of software anybody will ever use on these.

Keep the originals. Give out copies. I have given a set to the historical society and a set to the county clerk and one is at my sister's in Pell with the backup drive.

[b]Where they are going[/b]

The railfan people at [url=synth://forums.verityrail.org/]forums.verityrail.org[/url] have a thread and I have posted the crossing sets there, which is the right audience even though about a quarter of the replies are about whether the signal bridge at Bracken Lane is original.

It is not original. It is 1968. It is on a plate on the base and I photographed the plate.

The county wiki article on the railroad at [url=synth://wiki.gridfall.net/]wiki.gridfall.net[/url] currently has one photograph in it, which is somebody's scan of a postcard.

comments.author: dennis o.
comments.body: I worked that yard twenty-eight years. The plate is 1968 and the bridge replaced a wooden one that came down in the flood. You are the first person to check before arguing about it.

comments.author: H. Speltz
comments.body: The society has the set and it is catalogued. The tannery point is well taken and I am the one who took those thirty photographs in 1997. I have thought about the loading dock roughly once a month since.

posts.title: The county wiki needs citations more than it needs categories
posts.body:
I have been editing the county wiki at [url=synth://wiki.gridfall.net/]wiki.gridfall.net[/url] since 2004. Small edits mostly. Dates, spellings, the occasional thing I can check at the clerk's office on my lunch.

In the last six months there has been a push to categorise everything. Six categories became a discussion about eleven categories, and there is now a page about what belongs in Folklore versus what belongs in History, and that page has had more edits this year than the article on the 1994 flood.

I want to make the unpopular argument.

[b]A category is a filing decision. A citation is a fact.[/b]

If the flood article says the crest was 14.2 feet and nobody knows where that came from, the article is worthless no matter how well it is filed. If it says the crest was 14.2 feet according to the state gauge at the Mill Street bridge, reported in the Ledger on March 9 1994, then it is worth something even if it is filed under the wrong category, because the next person can check it.

Right now, by my count, thirty-one of the county wiki's articles contain a specific number and eleven of those say where the number came from.

[b]The fire article is the worst case[/b]

The article on the 2003 substation fire has a paragraph that has been reverted, by my count, nineteen times. Both versions are unsourced. It is two people rewriting each other's guess, forever, and every revert is logged and none of them has ever added a document.

The state commission published a two page summary in November 2003. It is a public record. It is in a filing cabinet at the clerk's office and I have photographed it. I put the citation in the article in April. It survived eleven days.

[b]What I am asking for[/b]

Nothing structural. No new template, no new policy page, no new category.

If you edit an article and you know where you got it, write where you got it in the sentence. That is it. "According to." Four extra words.

[b]The thing I will admit[/b]

I understand why people would rather argue about categories. Categories are a thing you can finish. Sourcing the county's history is not a thing anybody finishes and most of the documents are in a basement in Gridfall that floods.

I still think it is the job.

There is a thread about this on [url=synth://boards.gridfall.net/]boards.gridfall.net[/url] and a shorter and more civil version of it on [url=synth://pulse.gridfall.net/]pulse.gridfall.net[/url], and the ring at [url=synth://webring.gridfall.net/]webring.gridfall.net[/url] has about nine county sites on it that between them contain a great deal of primary material nobody has ever cited.

comments.author: H. Speltz
comments.body: The society will host scans of anything anybody cites, free, as long as we are allowed to keep a copy. That offer has been open since 2005 and has been taken up four times.

comments.author: webmaster_hs
comments.body: Categories are how people find articles. You do not get to call the finding mechanism frivolous because you personally arrive by typing the title.

comments.author: d.carrow
comments.body: That is a good objection and I do not have a great answer to it. I would still rather have eleven sourced articles in one bad category than forty unsourced ones filed perfectly.

comments.author: marla
comments.body: the diner article said 1959 for two years until you fixed it. that is the whole post in one line.
